The meaning is that the joints of the celestial spheres will come apart, and what has held this system together in an orderly way will be undone. It is a remarkable coincidence that today's astronomers, on the basis of their observations, have proposed a manner of the end of the present system which is exactly the same as what the Qur'an describes. Yet they reached these estimates purely through scientific observation. In any case, they have observed very little of this universe, and they have built these hypotheses upon that small observation.

However, we believers observe those hypotheses in these Qur'anic verses in a very detailed manner. These are extremely concise verses, and they describe not specific events but general and fundamental ones. We are content only with those fundamental events which the Qur'an has described. These are true reports for us, because these verses have been stated by the One who revealed the Qur'an and also created the universe, and who knows His creations far better than our limited observations. For in the universe of Allah, this earth, these mountains, and the sun together with the entire galaxy and stars are like the tiny particles of dust that fly about on the ground. Therefore, just as one of us can lift two particles and throw them away, for Allah lifting the earth and throwing it is like that. So on the Day of Resurrection, when the binding of the heavens is released, the earth and the heavens will fly about like particles, and these matters too are known from the living verses of the Qur'an.

Now the majesty of the Lord of Glory overspreads the scene, and after the blowing of the Trumpet, the crumbling of the earth and mountains into dust, and the quaking and disorder, a stillness descends upon this entire universe. And the greatness and magnificence of the Lord of Glory and Almighty overspreads everything.

The Angels will be on its sides, and eight of them will bear the Throne of your Lord above them that Day. (69:17)

The angels will be on the sides and borders of this universe and the heavens, and above this universe will be the Throne of God, which will be carried by eight angels. Will these eight be eight classes, or will they be eight known only to God as to what they will be? Who are these eight and what are they? We have no knowledge of their details either. We have no knowledge of the reality of the Throne, nor of the manner of its carrying. We set all these matters aside, because they belong to the unseen realm, the detailed knowledge of which has not been given to us, and God has neither made us responsible for acquiring detailed knowledge of these things nor commanded us to seek it. We leave these details also to God's unseen knowledge. Now, only God will remain, everything will perish, and this is the awareness which the Qur'an and this Surah wish to give us: that we fear God, fear accountability on the Day of Resurrection, and fear God's power and majesty.

Everyone will be laid bare and exposed: the body, the conscience, the deeds and the outcome. All the secrets that were behind veils will be brought out into the open. The human self will be naked, the human body will be naked, and human defects will come to light. Witnesses will come forward. Human cunning and craftiness will vanish. All stratagems and plans will become ineffective. Even the things that a person concealed from himself will be revealed. How great will be the shame when secrets are laid bare before all. How humiliated human beings will be in the eyes of people. As for Allah, everything was already open before Him; it is open even now. But the human mind does not hold this as a conscious reality, because his consciousness is shaped by the concealment practised between one human being and another on this earth, whereas on the Day of Judgement the only difference will be that the consciousness of the veil which that wretched human being held will be lifted, and he will think that all veils have fallen. In this universe everything is open. Now that the earth has been lifted up and flung down, all screens have been removed. It is level, an open plain. The bonds of the sky too will be opened, and nothing will remain hidden behind the heavens. Bodies are naked, human psychology is laid open; there is neither secret nor confidence left.

Yet this is an extremely distressing matter, greater than the whole earth and all the mountains. It is even more severe than the sky splitting asunder and falling in pieces, for a human being will stand completely naked: his psychological states will be exposed to people, his consciousness will become manifest, his entire history will be brought forward, all his misdeeds will be locked into a film, all his hidden matters will be disclosed, and all these affairs will be seen by the whole of humanity: before the angels, before the jinn, before humans. They will be beneath the Throne and the majesty of Allah's kingdom, and they will be greatly terrified.

Human temperament and psychology are extremely complex. Within human psychology there are countless ups and downs, within which lie the self, the inner states, and the inclinations and tendencies, good or bad. There are his capacities and his hidden secrets. (Tauqa'a Bamiyya, p. 18) Like the sea creature within its shell, which, when even a needle or thorn pricks it, quickly contracts and hides itself inside its shell, withdrawing completely within and shutting itself fully. Man does the same: when he learns that some eye is watching him, that all his movements are being recorded, and that what he has been concealing has already become apparent, he feels intense pain that his most private matters have been exposed.

Now consider that such a human being will on that day be naked, and naked in every respect: naked in body and heart, naked in consciousness, intention and conscience. He will be deprived of every veil. He will be under the judgement of Allah, the Almighty and Subduer, and will stand before all the people of the earth, the first and the last. This will certainly be a bitter condition, more bitter and harsh than anything. After this, the scene of those who attain salvation and those who are sent to Hell is presented, as though this scene were before one's eyes.

Here, sensory and material blessings are being enumerated before the listener, the kind of blessings the Arabs well understood as the pinnacle of material prosperity. Now this person knows that a decision has been made against him, and that his final end is the Fire of Hell. He stands in that arena with a most regrettable end, in a state of utter disintegration, and he is the one who makes the above remark.

The depiction of this person is very lengthy. His regret is described at some length, to such an extent that a reader feels this description will never end. The tone is also despairing. But this is the distinctive style of the Holy Qur'an: it extends some scenes and situations and describes others in a few sentences, and in this way it leaves very beneficial effects upon the human soul. The purpose here is to give thoughts of regret and remorse some length, so that people may consider now how much regret and shame will be faced there. The punishment is, of course, a far greater matter. Therefore this scene has been made somewhat long, because the main purpose in the context of the discourse was exactly this. In it there is also great reproach. This wretched person wishes, saying: "Would that this moment had never come! Would that I had not been given my record of deeds, and had not known what had happened! Would that this death had been final, and that the elements of my constitution had been brought to an end!" Further, there is grief upon him, because the things in which he took pride in the world are of absolutely no benefit to him.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 69, verses 28–29:

"My wealth has not availed me anything. My authority has gone from me." (69:28–29, Qur'an)

Not only that: my whole authority has perished. Neither wealth is of benefit nor has my authority been of benefit. The tone of the statement is filled with grief and despair. The rhyming endings that the Qur'an has chosen for it make it very long (in the way that someone weeps over a deceased person), so that at the end there is "hā" (ه), and before it "yā" (ي), and before that "alif" (ا): kitabiyah, hisabiyah, qadiyah, maliyah and sultaniyah. These words are also a kind of prolongation and are full of regret, and this is expressed in a most eloquent and articulate manner.

This extremely sorrowful tone ends at the moment when, from the court of Divine justice, a forceful decree is issued together with orders for its execution.

On the verses 33–34 of Surah al-Haqqah (69), which speak of the one who did not believe in Allah and did not urge feeding the needy:

He whose heart was empty of faith in Allah was not even a good human being by human standards. He did not show mercy to people. Therefore, there was no place fitting for him except this Fire.

The person whose heart is empty of faith is dead. His heart becomes a ruin, it is destroyed. There is no light within him; he has been distorted. He has become lower than the animals, and lower than inanimate things, because everything is a believer. Everything glorifies (Allah). Everything is connected to the true source of its existence. As for this intelligent human being, he cuts himself off from his origin and his source.

Then his heart does not feel compassion for people. The needy among the servants of Allah are in greater need of Allah's mercy. Their needs must be attended to. Caring for their lodging, food and clothing is the duty of us human beings. Thus it becomes clear that the collective economic needs of human beings are the responsibility of society, and that these are connected with matters of faith.

**Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 69, verse 37:**

﴿... no one eats it except the sinners﴾ (96:73) "Which no one eats except sinners": those whose nature is steeped in this sin.

These are the reasons why this person deserves to be seized, to have a chain put around his neck, and to be burned in the Fire, and why such long chains were placed on him. Hell, and chains within it, are among the most severe degrees of the punishment of Hell. This is the condition of the one who does not urge others to feed the needy. Now consider for yourselves the punishment of that "person" who keeps children, women and the elderly alive in hunger, who seizes their guardians unjustly like rebellious tyrants, who even snatches the morsels and clothing from their hands, leaving them under open sky in the harsh winter. Where will such "dictators" go, when they are found throughout the earth? Just think what Allah has prepared for them, when merely failing to urge people to feed the needy has been made the subject of such a severe punishment.

This harsh and impactful imagery is brought in this fierce Surah because it is a Surah of the early period, when Arab society was extremely harsh and rough. They needed to be shown such harsh scenes so that they would be somewhat frightened by them, would soften their conduct a little, and would strive to save themselves from that disgrace. Whenever humanity is in a diverse social condition of this kind, in which on one side there are harsh and rough people of this type, and on the other side there are gentle and receptive people alongside them, that is, where people's psychological states stand at different levels, the address of the Qur'an keeps all these people in view, and the call is presented in such a way that people of different levels can benefit from it. Even today there are hard-hearted people in some regions. There are also people of such temperament who are extremely hard, and only words that blaze can affect them, as in this Surah. They can only be frightened by the very scenes described in this Surah.

This is a very great oath. It is an oath by the great universe that you see, and an oath by the great universe that is not visible to you. This universe is far greater than what human observation can grasp; indeed it is far greater than what man can comprehend. Man can perceive only a very small part of this universe, and observe only a very small part of it. This indication greatly opens up the human heart and mind. ﴿So I swear by what you see, and by what you do not see.﴾ (69:38–39)

This and many similar verses point to this reality. Although some "insects," thinking "insects," still, in the name of science, keep the doors of the Lord's light closed upon themselves. These people are in truth neither scientists nor believers. Just as they are backward in the field of science, so they are backward in the field of religion, and unconsciously they are caught in the prison of materialism, and they have fallen behind the station and rank that befits a noble creature like man.

Let us reflect again:

﴿So I swear by what you see, and by what you do not see. Indeed it is the word of a noble Messenger, and it is not the word of a poet; little do you believe. Nor is it the word of a soothsayer; little do you reflect. It is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ (69:38–43)

Among the accusations that the polytheists of Makkah made against the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the Qur'an was that he was a poet. The second was that he was a soothsayer, and this was a superficial doubt. It arose for them because this Qur'an was an incomparable speech, and its standard was far higher than the speech of ordinary people. They used to say he was a poet because they imagined that poets are visited by jinn, and that they hear such speech from them. Likewise they considered soothsayers to have connections with the jinn, and believed that these matters were told to them by the jinn. This doubt was very superficial, and by reflecting upon the Qur'an, prophethood, and the person of the Messenger, it could quickly be dispelled.

It is true that in poetry there is sometimes good music, lofty ideas, and beauty, but the Qur'an and poetry are completely different things. There is a fundamental difference between the two. The noble Qur'an provides a complete system of life, and this system is based upon truth. Its foundation rests upon the doctrine of *tawhid* (the oneness of God). It regards faith in one Creator of this universe as essential. It considers this universe, like human beings, to be living and obedient to its Lord. Whereas poetry consists of a few impressions, emotions, and scattered events. It has no connection with a system of life. It is not based upon a single doctrine that remains the same in joy and sorrow, in freedom and captivity, and in love and hatred; whereas poetry changes entirely under these conditions and differs in different circumstances.

Moreover, the worldview that the Qur'an presents has its first foundation laid by Islam and the Qur'an. Its details and its principles were all given by the Qur'an, and given with the belief that they all come from Allah. The method (manhaj) of such a worldview is of a kind that cannot be human. No human being can devise a comprehensive system and conception that has no precedent before it and none after it. By contrast, the philosophies that human beings have fabricated about this universe, its creative power and its governing power are also before us. They are described in detail in books on philosophy, poetry, and other intellectual and ideological schools. When they are studied comparatively with the Qur'an, it becomes clear that the Qur'an is entirely the outpouring of a separate source. It has a unique temperament and unique characteristics, and compared to it, human conceptions are like a patchwork of rags.

In the same way, regarding what is transmitted from soothsayers (kuhhan, pl. of kahin, a diviner who claimed knowledge of the unseen), no soothsayer has appeared in human history who gave a system of life, a philosophy of life, and a system of the Hereafter that was as complete, perfect, and reasonable as the system presented by the Qur'an. What has been transmitted from soothsayers is this: some meaningless utterances, rhymed prose (saj') and rhyming phrases in which guesses are thrown together, and perhaps now and then some words of wisdom heard from elsewhere.

However, there are within the Qur'an certain glimpses which, upon reflection, clearly show that a human being could never think in this manner. In *Fi Zilal al-Qur'an* we have shown some such glimpses, that neither before the Qur'an nor after it has the human mind ever gone in that direction. Some verses are presented here for consideration as well.

﴿With Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them but He. He knows whatever is on the land and in the sea. Not a leaf falls but He knows it, nor is there a grain in the darkness of the earth, nor anything moist or dry, but it is in a clear Book.﴾ (6:95)

For example, this conception:

﴿He knows what enters the earth and what comes out of it, what descends from the sky and what ascends into it. And He is with you wherever you are, and He sees whatever you do.﴾ (75:4) Or, for instance, a thought of this kind:

﴿No female conceives, nor gives birth, except with His knowledge. No one is granted a long life, nor is any life shortened, except that it is all written in a Book. Indeed, that is easy for Allah.﴾ (53:11)

Furthermore, no human being had ever given thought to how Allah holds this universe together, nor will anyone do so afterward.

﴿Indeed, it is Allah who holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease. And if they were to cease, none could hold them after Him.﴾ (53:14)

Or this scene: how life bursts forth in this universe, and what arrangements the Creator of the universe has made for the establishment of life here, and how He has made conditions suitable:

﴿Indeed, Allah splits the grain and the date-stone. He brings the living out of the dead, and He brings the dead out of the living. That is Allah. How then are you deluded? He splits the darkness of dawn and makes the night a time of rest. He has appointed the sun and the moon with precise reckoning. These are the decrees of the Mighty, the All-Knowing. And it is He who made the stars for you, that you may find your way by them in the darkness of land and sea. We have made the signs clear for a people who know. And it is He who created you from a single soul, then there is a place of settlement and a place of entrusting for you. We have made the signs clear for a people who understand. And it is He who sends down water from the sky, and by it We bring forth vegetation of every kind. From it We bring forth green plants, from which We produce layered grain, and from the spathes of the date-palm clusters of dates hanging low. And gardens of grapes, olives and pomegranates, similar yet varied. Look at their fruit when they bear fruit and ripen. Indeed, in these there are signs for a people who believe.﴾ (6:99)

Such glimpses are very abundant in the Qur'an, and such matters do not occur in human thought or in human styles of speech. These aspects of the Qur'an alone are sufficient proof that this Qur'an is from Allah. Even if one sets aside the other proofs, both those within this Book and those in the circumstances in which it was revealed, there are within this Book matters to which the human mind would never turn. Therefore, the doubts of these people were superficial, and they voiced them at a time when only some surahs of the Qur'an had been revealed; the whole Qur'an was not yet complete. Even at that time this distinctive quality was present in the Qur'an. Within it were clear indications that its source is not on earth, but in heaven.

The chiefs of Quraysh felt this in their hearts, and at times they even acknowledged it among themselves. But self-interest blinds a person, and one whose sights are set on worldly gain cannot decide to walk the path of guidance. The Qur'an had foretold regarding such circumstances that they would now level accusations of this kind, saying that it is an ancient falsehood.

Many events have been transmitted in the books of Seerah (the biography of the Prophet ﷺ) that when the leaders of Quraysh spoke among themselves about this matter, they themselves admitted that their statement was wrong.

Ibn Ishaq has transmitted this narration concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, and Utbah ibn Rabi'ah. Of these, he has transmitted the following about the first person:

"Then it happened that some people of Quraysh gathered at the house of al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah. He was an elderly man, and the season of Hajj was approaching, during which delegations from all over the Arab world would come to you, and all the Arabs have heard reports about this man of yours. So gather your opinions and speak with one voice, and do not say contradictory things about him, lest your statements refute one another and you contradict yourselves." They said, "O Abu Abd al-Shams, you speak first and settle a matter for us, and we will act accordingly." He said, "First you tell me what your opinions are." Some said, "We will say that he is a soothsayer." He said, "No, by God, he is not a soothsayer. We have seen soothsayers. His speech is not like the mumbling of soothsayers, nor is there in it the rhymed prose of soothsayers." Then they said, "We will say that he is possessed (majnun)." He said, "He is not possessed either. We have seen the possessed, and we know them. He does not have their fits, nor does he suffer their whisperings, nor is he afflicted by delusions." Some said, "Then let us call him a poet." He said, "He is not a poet. We all know poets, and the forms of poetry: rajaz, hazaj, qarid, maqbud, mabsut. So the Qur'an is not of these." Then they said, "Then let us call him a magician and a sorcerer." He said, "He is not a sorcerer either. We have seen sorcerers; he does not blow as they blow, nor does he tie knots as they do." After that they said, "Abu Abd al-Shams, you tell us what we should call him." He said, "By God, his words are extremely sweet, its roots are deep and its branches spread wide, and there is fruit upon its branches. Whatever you say of it, people will know that it is false. The nearest thing that can be said is that he is a sorcerer who has brought a magic that separates a son from his father, a brother from his brother, a husband from his wife, and a man from his family." So they went away and sat along the roads of Makkah. When the people came for Hajj, whoever came they would speak to him about Muhammad ﷺ and frighten people away from him.

And it is related about Nadr ibn al-Harith that he said: "O people of Quraysh! By God, a calamity has befallen you for which you have no remedy. Muhammad was a small young boy among you, the most beloved of you, the most truthful of you, the most trustworthy of you. When you saw gray hair on his temples and he brought to you what he brought, you said, 'He is a sorcerer.' No, by God, he is not a sorcerer. We have seen sorcerers, and their blowing and their knots we have seen. You said, 'He is a soothsayer.' No, by God, he is not a soothsayer. We have seen soothsayers, and their trances we have seen, and we have heard their rhymed speech. You say, 'He is a poet.' No, by God, he is not; he is not a poet. We have seen poets, and we are acquainted with the forms of poetry: rajaz, hazaj, and so on. You say, 'He is possessed.' We have seen the possessed; he has no fits, nor is he a victim of whisperings, nor are his words confused. O company of Quraysh! Reflect on this matter of yours. By God, I think a great calamity has come upon you..."

The statements of Nadr and Utbah are in complete agreement. It is also possible that this was one single event, which was sometimes attributed to Utbah and sometimes to Nadr. But it is not unlikely that both said something similar, since both were among the notables of Quraysh, and their impressions of the Qur'an were alike.

The position that Utbah took was narrated earlier by us in the introduction to Surah al-Qalam. His stance regarding the Prophet ﷺ and the Qur'an was very close to that of al-Walid and al-Nadr.

In short, when these people made the accusation that you are a sorcerer or a soothsayer, sometimes they said this out of cunning and deceit, and sometimes they did it merely to create confusion. And they never succeeded in this, because the Qur'an itself was so clear that people understood it as soon as they heard it. Therefore it had no need for an oath, that Allah should swear by things that are known and things that are not known. (According to Sayyid Qutb, the meaning of the verses would be: "I do not swear." But the translation of the Indian scholars is correct: "Nay, I swear.")

Indeed, this is the word of the Messenger of Noble Lineage ﷺ. It is not the speech of a poet, nor the speech of a soothsayer. It is sent down from the Lord of the worlds.

The statement here that this is the word of the Noble Messenger ﷺ does not mean that the Noble Messenger ﷺ composed this speech. The meaning is that this is a different kind of speech. Poets and soothsayers cannot produce such speech; only a Messenger can produce such speech. Allah sent him and revealed this to him, and therefore it was immediately said afterward:

﴿It is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ (96:34)

And these following remarks:

﴿Little is it that you believe﴾ (96:24) ﴿Little is it that you take heed﴾ (96:24). Their purpose is that you do not believe at all, and you do not take heed at all. This manner of expression was common in the Arabic language for complete negation, where complete negation was expressed by the word "little." It is related in a hadith that the Prophet ﷺ was "little in idle talk," meaning that he did not engage in idle talk at all. Here the intention is complete negation. Otherwise, if someone had even a little faith, and took even a little admonition from the Qur'an, he could not call the Messenger of Allah a poet or a soothsayer. Only an unbeliever and a heedless person could say such a thing about the Prophet ﷺ.

Finally, there comes this terrifying warning: whoever fabricates a falsehood against Allah regarding the faith will be seized by Allah. This threat also negates the one possibility that remains, namely that the Prophet ﷺ might have made this up himself. So Allah says that you are truthful, and if he had fabricated any falsehood against Us, We would have seized him with severity. Among Islamic beliefs, whoever makes even a slight distortion is seized.

﴿So I swear by what you see, and by what you do not see. Indeed it is the word of a noble Messenger, and it is not the word of a poet; little do you believe. Nor is it the word of a soothsayer; little do you reflect. It is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ (69:38–43)

It arose for them because this Qur'an was an incomparable speech, and its standard was far higher than the speech of ordinary people. They used to say he was a poet because they imagined that poets are visited by jinn, and that they hear such speech from them. It is true that in poetry there is sometimes good music, lofty ideas, and beauty, but the Qur'an and poetry are completely different things. There is a fundamental difference between the two. The noble Qur'an provides a complete system of life, and this system is based upon truth. Its foundation rests upon the doctrine of *tawhid* (the oneness of God). It regards faith in one Creator of this universe as essential. It considers this universe, like human beings, to be living and obedient to its Lord. Whereas poetry consists of a few impressions, emotions, and scattered events. It has no connection with a system of life. It is not based upon a single doctrine that remains the same in joy and sorrow, in freedom and captivity, and in love and hatred; whereas poetry changes entirely under these conditions and differs in different circumstances.

Moreover, the worldview that the Qur'an presents has its first foundation laid by Islam and the Qur'an. Its details and its principles were all given by the Qur'an, and given with the belief that they all come from Allah. The method (manhaj) of such a worldview is of a kind that cannot be human. No human being can devise a comprehensive system and conception that has no precedent before it and none after it. By contrast, the philosophies that human beings have fabricated about this universe, its creative power and its governing power are also before us. They are described in detail in books on philosophy, poetry, and other intellectual and ideological schools. When they are studied comparatively with the Qur'an, it becomes clear that the Qur'an is entirely the outpouring of a separate source. It has a unique temperament and unique characteristics, and compared to it, human conceptions are like a patchwork of rags.

However, there are within the Qur'an certain glimpses which, upon reflection, clearly show that a human being could never think in this manner. In *Fi Zilal al-Qur'an* we have shown some such glimpses, that neither before the Qur'an nor after it has the human mind ever gone in that direction. Some verses are presented here for consideration as well.

﴿With Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them but He. He knows whatever is on the land and in the sea. Not a leaf falls but He knows it, nor is there a grain in the darkness of the earth, nor anything moist or dry, but it is in a clear Book.﴾ (6:95)

For example, this conception:

﴿He knows what enters the earth and what comes out of it, what descends from the sky and what ascends into it. And He is with you wherever you are, and He sees whatever you do.﴾ (75:4) Or, for instance, a thought of this kind:

﴿No female conceives, nor gives birth, except with His knowledge. No one is granted a long life, nor is any life shortened, except that it is all written in a Book. Indeed, that is easy for Allah.﴾ (53:11)

Furthermore, no human being had ever given thought to how Allah holds this universe together, nor will anyone do so afterward.

﴿Indeed, it is Allah who holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease. And if they were to cease, none could hold them after Him.﴾ (53:14)

Or this scene: how life bursts forth in this universe, and what arrangements the Creator of the universe has made for the establishment of life here, and how He has made conditions suitable:

﴿Indeed, Allah splits the grain and the date-stone. He brings the living out of the dead, and He brings the dead out of the living. That is Allah. How then are you deluded? These aspects of the Qur'an alone are sufficient proof that this Qur'an is from Allah. Even if one sets aside the other proofs, both those within this Book and those in the circumstances in which it was revealed, there are within this Book matters to which the human mind would never turn. We have seen poets, and we are acquainted with the forms of poetry: rajaz, hazaj, and so on. You say, 'He is possessed.' The statements of Nadr and Utbah are in complete agreement. It is also possible that this was one single event, which was sometimes attributed to Utbah and sometimes to Nadr. But it is not unlikely that both said something similar, since both were among the notables of Quraysh, and their impressions of the Qur'an were alike.

The position that Utbah took was narrated earlier by us in the introduction to Surah al-Qalam. His stance regarding the Prophet ﷺ and the Qur'an was very close to that of al-Walid and al-Nadr.

In short, when these people made the accusation that you are a sorcerer or a soothsayer, sometimes they said this out of cunning and deceit, and sometimes they did it merely to create confusion. And they never succeeded in this, because the Qur'an itself was so clear that people understood it as soon as they heard it. Therefore it had no need for an oath, that Allah should swear by things that are known and things that are not known. (According to Sayyid Qutb, the meaning of the verses would be: "I do not swear." But the translation of the Indian scholars is correct: "Nay, I swear.")

Indeed, this is the word of the Messenger of Noble Lineage ﷺ. It is not the speech of a poet, nor the speech of a soothsayer. It is sent down from the Lord of the worlds.

The statement here that this is the word of the Noble Messenger ﷺ does not mean that the Noble Messenger ﷺ composed this speech. The meaning is that this is a different kind of speech. Poets and soothsayers cannot produce such speech; only a Messenger can produce such speech. Allah sent him and revealed this to him, and therefore it was immediately said afterward:

﴿It is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ (96:34)

And these following remarks:

﴿Little is it that you believe﴾ (96:24) ﴿Little is it that you take heed﴾ (96:24). Their purpose is that you do not believe at all, and you do not take heed at all. This manner of expression was common in the Arabic language for complete negation, where complete negation was expressed by the word "little." It is related in a hadith that the Prophet ﷺ was "little in idle talk," meaning that he did not engage in idle talk at all. Here the intention is complete negation. Otherwise, if someone had even a little faith, and took even a little admonition from the Qur'an, he could not call the Messenger of Allah a poet or a soothsayer. Only an unbeliever and a heedless person could say such a thing about the Prophet ﷺ.

Finally, there comes this terrifying warning: whoever fabricates a falsehood against Allah regarding the faith will be seized by Allah. This threat also negates the one possibility that remains, namely that the Prophet ﷺ might have made this up himself. So Allah says that you are truthful, and if he had fabricated any falsehood against Us, We would have seized him with severity. Among Islamic beliefs, whoever makes even a slight distortion is seized.

This matter is very clear. It needs no oath, it is established by reason, and it is a fact. There is no need at all to swear an oath about it. It is the truth, revealed from the Truth. It is neither poetry nor the soothsaying (*kahanah*, the utterances of a soothsayer) and ramblings of a *kahin* (soothsayer), nor the fabrication of an inventor of lies. Therefore there is no need for an oath.

This is a very great oath. It is an oath by the great universe that you see, and an oath by the great universe that is not visible to you. This universe is far greater than what human observation can grasp; indeed it is far greater than what man can comprehend. Man can perceive only a very small part of this universe, and observe only a very small part of it. God has given man only as much capacity as he needs to live on this earth, to develop it, and to be the vicegerent (*khalifah*, representative) of God here. If the whole earth is compared with the whole universe, it is a tiny particle, not even visible from the far end of this universe. Of this vast divine universe, human beings have been given the insight and vision of only a very limited portion. Man has so far been able to learn only a very small part of its secrets, its conditions, and the laws of nature. A very large part remains that man cannot see.

﴿Fa-la uqsimu bi-ma tubsirun wa ma la tubsirun﴾: "So I swear by what you see, and by what you do not see." (69:38–39)

This indication greatly opens up the human heart and mind. When a person finds that beyond the present scope of human thought and vision there are other dimensions, other worlds, and hidden secrets that man cannot yet see, then the scope of human imagination and perception expands. The horizons of this universe become wider. Therefore a person who lives and dwells in this Qur'an is not bound by the limited space in which he lives. He is not a prisoner of the narrow range of his eyes, nor does he rest content with his present limited perception. This universe is wider than our observation, and this reality is greater than our power of perception. Because the limited vision and perceptive faculty given to this limited human being was given for his limited needs in this world. Yet he can expand his vision and his perceptive faculty, and he can also expand these limited powers. But he can do so only when he becomes aware that there are realities and worlds beyond, which we have not yet reached, and that behind the veil there are worlds far wider than those we have reached. Here, a person's connection with that Absolute Being is established, who bestows light upon man, and through a direct connection with Him, man then travels through other worlds which are apparently hidden.

Those who confine themselves to the realities that the eye can see, or that our perceptive faculty can grasp, are in truth poor and wretched. In reality, such people are prisoners of their extremely limited sensations and perceptions. Such people live in this vast world, yet they have made themselves like the frog in the well, whereas man has been sent into a great universe so that he may observe it and take a lesson.

Throughout human history, within this universe and upon this earth, it has often happened that some people have made themselves frogs in a well in this way. They have closed upon themselves the doors of recognition and light, and they have deprived themselves of reaching the Supreme Reality through the path of faith and consciousness. Then they begin to try to close these doors of light upon others too, just as they closed them upon themselves. At times they have done this in the name of *jahiliyyah* (the age of ignorance), and at other times in the name of atheism (*ladiniyyah*). Both *jahiliyyah* and modern scientific *jahiliyyah* are in truth one great prison, within which these people have confined themselves, and they have deprived themselves of the true sources of recognition and light.

Over the last two hundred years, Western science, because of its pride and folly, had shut itself behind these strong bars. But in this century, Western science itself has gradually begun to break these strong bars and to connect its own experiments with the sources of light. This became possible when the fervour and pride of science cooled, and it emerged from the intoxication of the follies of the Church and of its frenzy of revenge against it. (*Insan, Maddiyyat aur Islam ke Darmiyan*, Muhammad Qutb)

Science also came to know that within this universe its limits of operation are limited, and it experienced that these limited instruments through which it observes this universe are themselves leading it toward some unlimited universe. Thus science has begun to call people to faith. (*Science ki taraf se Da'wat-e-Iman*, translated by Mahmud Falaki, authored by A. Gracie)

In a most humble manner, science gave good news and announced that it has now been released from this prison. Whenever humanity has shut itself behind the bars of materialism, the same treatment has befallen it.

This universe is far greater than what human observation can grasp; indeed it is far greater than what man can comprehend. This indication greatly opens up the human heart and mind. This and many similar verses point to this reality. Although some "insects," thinking "insects," still, in the name of science, keep the doors of the Lord's light closed upon themselves. ﴿So I swear by what you see, and by what you do not see. Indeed it is the word of a noble Messenger, and it is not the word of a poet; little do you believe. Nor is it the word of a soothsayer; little do you reflect. It is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ (69:38–43)

Among the accusations that the polytheists of Makkah made against the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the Qur'an was that he was a poet. The second was that he was a soothsayer, and this was a superficial doubt. It arose for them because this Qur'an was an incomparable speech, and its standard was far higher than the speech of ordinary people. They used to say he was a poet because they imagined that poets are visited by jinn, and that they hear such speech from them. Likewise they considered soothsayers to have connections with the jinn, and believed that these matters were told to them by the jinn. This doubt was very superficial, and by reflecting upon the Qur'an, prophethood, and the person of the Messenger, it could quickly be dispelled.

It is true that in poetry there is sometimes good music, lofty ideas, and beauty, but the Qur'an and poetry are completely different things. There is a fundamental difference between the two. The noble Qur'an provides a complete system of life, and this system is based upon truth. Its foundation rests upon the doctrine of *tawhid* (the oneness of God). It regards faith in one Creator of this universe as essential. It considers this universe, like human beings, to be living and obedient to its Lord. Whereas poetry consists of a few impressions, emotions, and scattered events. It has no connection with a system of life. It is not based upon a single doctrine that remains the same in joy and sorrow, in freedom and captivity, and in love and hatred; whereas poetry changes entirely under these conditions and differs in different circumstances.

Moreover, the worldview that the Qur'an presents has its first foundation laid by Islam and the Qur'an. Its details and its principles were all given by the Qur'an, and given with the belief that they all come from Allah. The method (manhaj) of such a worldview is of a kind that cannot be human. No human being can devise a comprehensive system and conception that has no precedent before it and none after it. By contrast, the philosophies that human beings have fabricated about this universe, its creative power and its governing power are also before us. They are described in detail in books on philosophy, poetry, and other intellectual and ideological schools. When they are studied comparatively with the Qur'an, it becomes clear that the Qur'an is entirely the outpouring of a separate source. It has a unique temperament and unique characteristics, and compared to it, human conceptions are like a patchwork of rags.

In the same way, regarding what is transmitted from soothsayers (kuhhan, pl. of kahin, a diviner who claimed knowledge of the unseen), no soothsayer has appeared in human history who gave a system of life, a philosophy of life, and a system of the Hereafter that was as complete, perfect, and reasonable as the system presented by the Qur'an. What has been transmitted from soothsayers is this: some meaningless utterances, rhymed prose (saj') and rhyming phrases in which guesses are thrown together, and perhaps now and then some words of wisdom heard from elsewhere.

However, there are within the Qur'an certain glimpses which, upon reflection, clearly show that a human being could never think in this manner. In *Fi Zilal al-Qur'an* we have shown some such glimpses, that neither before the Qur'an nor after it has the human mind ever gone in that direction. Some verses are presented here for consideration as well.

﴿With Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them but He. He knows whatever is on the land and in the sea. Not a leaf falls but He knows it, nor is there a grain in the darkness of the earth, nor anything moist or dry, but it is in a clear Book.﴾ (6:95)

For example, this conception:

﴿He knows what enters the earth and what comes out of it, what descends from the sky and what ascends into it. And He is with you wherever you are, and He sees whatever you do.﴾ (75:4) Or, for instance, a thought of this kind:

﴿No female conceives, nor gives birth, except with His knowledge. No one is granted a long life, nor is any life shortened, except that it is all written in a Book. Indeed, that is easy for Allah.﴾ (53:11)

Furthermore, no human being had ever given thought to how Allah holds this universe together, nor will anyone do so afterward.

﴿Indeed, it is Allah who holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease. And if they were to cease, none could hold them after Him.﴾ (53:14)

Or this scene: how life bursts forth in this universe, and what arrangements the Creator of the universe has made for the establishment of life here, and how He has made conditions suitable:

﴿Indeed, Allah splits the grain and the date-stone. He brings the living out of the dead, and He brings the dead out of the living. That is Allah. How then are you deluded? He splits the darkness of dawn and makes the night a time of rest. He has appointed the sun and the moon with precise reckoning. These are the decrees of the Mighty, the All-Knowing. And it is He who made the stars for you, that you may find your way by them in the darkness of land and sea. We have made the signs clear for a people who know. And it is He who created you from a single soul, then there is a place of settlement and a place of entrusting for you. We have made the signs clear for a people who understand. And it is He who sends down water from the sky, and by it We bring forth vegetation of every kind. From it We bring forth green plants, from which We produce layered grain, and from the spathes of the date-palm clusters of dates hanging low. And gardens of grapes, olives and pomegranates, similar yet varied. Look at their fruit when they bear fruit and ripen. Indeed, in these there are signs for a people who believe.﴾ (6:99)

Such glimpses are very abundant in the Qur'an, and such matters do not occur in human thought or in human styles of speech. These aspects of the Qur'an alone are sufficient proof that this Qur'an is from Allah. Even if one sets aside the other proofs, both those within this Book and those in the circumstances in which it was revealed, there are within this Book matters to which the human mind would never turn. Therefore, the doubts of these people were superficial, and they voiced them at a time when only some surahs of the Qur'an had been revealed; the whole Qur'an was not yet complete. Even at that time this distinctive quality was present in the Qur'an. Within it were clear indications that its source is not on earth, but in heaven.

The chiefs of Quraysh felt this in their hearts, and at times they even acknowledged it among themselves. But self-interest blinds a person, and one whose sights are set on worldly gain cannot decide to walk the path of guidance. The Qur'an had foretold regarding such circumstances that they would now level accusations of this kind, saying that it is an ancient falsehood.

Many events have been transmitted in the books of Seerah (the biography of the Prophet ﷺ) that when the leaders of Quraysh spoke among themselves about this matter, they themselves admitted that their statement was wrong.

Ibn Ishaq has transmitted this narration concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, and Utbah ibn Rabi'ah. Of these, he has transmitted the following about the first person:

"Then it happened that some people of Quraysh gathered at the house of al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah. He was an elderly man, and the season of Hajj was approaching, during which delegations from all over the Arab world would come to you, and all the Arabs have heard reports about this man of yours. So gather your opinions and speak with one voice, and do not say contradictory things about him, lest your statements refute one another and you contradict yourselves." They said, "O Abu Abd al-Shams, you speak first and settle a matter for us, and we will act accordingly." He said, "First you tell me what your opinions are." Some said, "We will say that he is a soothsayer." He said, "No, by God, he is not a soothsayer. We have seen soothsayers. His speech is not like the mumbling of soothsayers, nor is there in it the rhymed prose of soothsayers." Then they said, "We will say that he is possessed (majnun)." He said, "He is not possessed either. We have seen the possessed, and we know them. He does not have their fits, nor does he suffer their whisperings, nor is he afflicted by delusions." Some said, "Then let us call him a poet." He said, "He is not a poet. We all know poets, and the forms of poetry: rajaz, hazaj, qarid, maqbud, mabsut. So the Qur'an is not of these." Then they said, "Then let us call him a magician and a sorcerer." He said, "He is not a sorcerer either. We have seen sorcerers; he does not blow as they blow, nor does he tie knots as they do." After that they said, "Abu Abd al-Shams, you tell us what we should call him." He said, "By God, his words are extremely sweet, its roots are deep and its branches spread wide, and there is fruit upon its branches. Whatever you say of it, people will know that it is false. The nearest thing that can be said is that he is a sorcerer who has brought a magic that separates a son from his father, a brother from his brother, a husband from his wife, and a man from his family." So they went away and sat along the roads of Makkah. When the people came for Hajj, whoever came they would speak to him about Muhammad ﷺ and frighten people away from him.

And it is related about Nadr ibn al-Harith that he said: "O people of Quraysh! By God, a calamity has befallen you for which you have no remedy. Muhammad was a small young boy among you, the most beloved of you, the most truthful of you, the most trustworthy of you. When you saw gray hair on his temples and he brought to you what he brought, you said, 'He is a sorcerer.' No, by God, he is not a sorcerer. We have seen sorcerers, and their blowing and their knots we have seen. You said, 'He is a soothsayer.' No, by God, he is not a soothsayer. We have seen soothsayers, and their trances we have seen, and we have heard their rhymed speech. You say, 'He is a poet.' No, by God, he is not; he is not a poet. We have seen poets, and we are acquainted with the forms of poetry: rajaz, hazaj, and so on. You say, 'He is possessed.' We have seen the possessed; he has no fits, nor is he a victim of whisperings, nor are his words confused. O company of Quraysh! Reflect on this matter of yours. By God, I think a great calamity has come upon you..."

The statements of Nadr and Utbah are in complete agreement. It is also possible that this was one single event, which was sometimes attributed to Utbah and sometimes to Nadr. But it is not unlikely that both said something similar, since both were among the notables of Quraysh, and their impressions of the Qur'an were alike.

The position that Utbah took was narrated earlier by us in the introduction to Surah al-Qalam. His stance regarding the Prophet ﷺ and the Qur'an was very close to that of al-Walid and al-Nadr.

In short, when these people made the accusation that you are a sorcerer or a soothsayer, sometimes they said this out of cunning and deceit, and sometimes they did it merely to create confusion. Electricity, although inconceivable, is an established reality, and it is more established than a piece of wood which can be conceived." (*Beesvin Sadi ke Mufakkireen ke Aqaid*, Ustad Anad)

Sir Arthur Thomson, a famous author from Scotland, says: "We are living in an age in which this reality has become solid and transparent. Ether has lost its material existence. In the matter of excessive material interpretations, it is *hadith al-'ahd* (newly acquainted)."

In a collection of essays titled "Science and Religion," he says:

"Scholars of theology should not lament that a physicist does not get beyond the realm of physics to reach the Lord of physics. The reason is that scientific research does not have a theological direction. But if the scholars of physics were to go beyond the realm of physics and enter metaphysics, the results would be extremely great. After research up to today, we have become capable of expressing joy that scientists have provided the path to work in that direction, so that now religious feelings can breathe within science, whereas in the time of our forefathers it was not possible to speak of religion in scientific matters. Just as Mr. Lanchrous Defiss, in his book, made that false claim, in contrast to it we can now say with great force and confidence that science has paved the way for the most exalted and most lofty conception of God Almighty. And now we consider the literal meaning of this saying correct: that science has created for human beings a new heaven and a new earth, and has advanced the human intellect in struggle so far that at times it seems that man will find peace and safety only in the event that he believes in the Being of God." (*Daur-e-Jadid ke Mufakkireen ke Aqaid*, Ustad Anad)

Earlier we have quoted this extract from the book of A. Gracie Morrison, President of the Science Academy of New York and a member of the Executive Council of National Research in America. The book is titled "Man Does Not Stand Alone":

"We have in fact come close to a vast unknown world, because it has been scientifically proven that matter is in fact a manifestation of the cosmic age, and that in its reality it is energy. But there is no doubt that no chance or accident has any role in bringing this universe into existence, because this marvellous, vast universe is bound by an order."

"That this man was an animal who became a 'being' that is conscious, thinking, and aware of its own existence, is not correct, that this man became such merely due to material factors and that behind it there was no intention or will of a Creator. This is not a possible thing."

"If intention and will are accepted, then according to it man would be a machine, and the question would be who operates this machine, because without operation no benefit from it is evident. Science is unable to explain who is the director of the human machine, and moreover science cannot claim that will is a material thing."

"We have reached the point where we can say that God has given a part of His light to man."

It appears that science has now come out of the prison of materialism by breaking its bars and bringing down its walls, and it now thinks freely in the open air. Just as the Qur'an said:

﴿So I swear by what you see, and by what you do not see.﴾ (69:38–39)

This and many similar verses point to this reality. Although some "insects," thinking "insects," still, in the name of science, keep the doors of the Lord's light closed upon themselves. These people are in truth neither scientists nor believers. Just as they are backward in the field of science, so they are backward in the field of religion, and unconsciously they are caught in the prison of materialism, and they have fallen behind the station and rank that befits a noble creature like man.

Let us reflect again:

﴿So I swear by what you see, and by what you do not see. Indeed it is the word of a noble Messenger, and it is not the word of a poet; little do you believe. Nor is it the word of a soothsayer; little do you reflect. It is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ (69:38–43)

Among the accusations that the polytheists of Makkah made against the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the Qur'an was that he was a poet. The second was that he was a soothsayer, and this was a superficial doubt. It arose for them because this Qur'an was an incomparable speech, and its standard was far higher than the speech of ordinary people. They used to say he was a poet because they imagined that poets are visited by jinn, and that they hear such speech from them. Likewise they considered soothsayers to have connections with the jinn, and believed that these matters were told to them by the jinn. This doubt was very superficial, and by reflecting upon the Qur'an, prophethood, and the person of the Messenger, it could quickly be dispelled.

It is true that in poetry there is sometimes good music, lofty ideas, and beauty, but the Qur'an and poetry are completely different things. There is a fundamental difference between the two. The noble Qur'an provides a complete system of life, and this system is based upon truth. Its foundation rests upon the doctrine of *tawhid* (the oneness of God). It regards faith in one Creator of this universe as essential. It considers this universe, like human beings, to be living and obedient to its Lord. Whereas poetry consists of a few impressions, emotions, and scattered events. It has no connection with a system of life. It is not based upon a single doctrine that remains the same in joy and sorrow, in freedom and captivity, and in love and hatred; whereas poetry changes entirely under these conditions and differs in different circumstances.

Moreover, the worldview that the Qur'an presents has its first foundation laid by Islam and the Qur'an. Its details and its principles were all given by the Qur'an, and given with the belief that they all come from Allah. The method (manhaj) of such a worldview is of a kind that cannot be human. No human being can devise a comprehensive system and conception that has no precedent before it and none after it. By contrast, the philosophies that human beings have fabricated about this universe, its creative power and its governing power are also before us. They are described in detail in books on philosophy, poetry, and other intellectual and ideological schools. When they are studied comparatively with the Qur'an, it becomes clear that the Qur'an is entirely the outpouring of a separate source. It has a unique temperament and unique characteristics, and compared to it, human conceptions are like a patchwork of rags.

In the same way, regarding what is transmitted from soothsayers (kuhhan, pl. of kahin, a diviner who claimed knowledge of the unseen), no soothsayer has appeared in human history who gave a system of life, a philosophy of life, and a system of the Hereafter that was as complete, perfect, and reasonable as the system presented by the Qur'an. What has been transmitted from soothsayers is this: some meaningless utterances, rhymed prose (saj') and rhyming phrases in which guesses are thrown together, and perhaps now and then some words of wisdom heard from elsewhere.

However, there are within the Qur'an certain glimpses which, upon reflection, clearly show that a human being could never think in this manner. In *Fi Zilal al-Qur'an* we have shown some such glimpses, that neither before the Qur'an nor after it has the human mind ever gone in that direction. Some verses are presented here for consideration as well.

﴿With Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them but He. He knows whatever is on the land and in the sea. Not a leaf falls but He knows it, nor is there a grain in the darkness of the earth, nor anything moist or dry, but it is in a clear Book.﴾ (6:95)

For example, this conception:

﴿He knows what enters the earth and what comes out of it, what descends from the sky and what ascends into it. And He is with you wherever you are, and He sees whatever you do.﴾ (75:4) Or, for instance, a thought of this kind:

﴿No female conceives, nor gives birth, except with His knowledge. No one is granted a long life, nor is any life shortened, except that it is all written in a Book. Indeed, that is easy for Allah.﴾ (53:11)

Furthermore, no human being had ever given thought to how Allah holds this universe together, nor will anyone do so afterward.

﴿Indeed, it is Allah who holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease. And if they were to cease, none could hold them after Him.﴾ (53:14)

Or this scene: how life bursts forth in this universe, and what arrangements the Creator of the universe has made for the establishment of life here, and how He has made conditions suitable:

﴿Indeed, Allah splits the grain and the date-stone. He brings the living out of the dead, and He brings the dead out of the living. That is Allah. How then are you deluded? He splits the darkness of dawn and makes the night a time of rest. He has appointed the sun and the moon with precise reckoning. These are the decrees of the Mighty, the All-Knowing. And it is He who made the stars for you, that you may find your way by them in the darkness of land and sea. We have made the signs clear for a people who know. And it is He who created you from a single soul, then there is a place of settlement and a place of entrusting for you. We have made the signs clear for a people who understand. And it is He who sends down water from the sky, and by it We bring forth vegetation of every kind. From it We bring forth green plants, from which We produce layered grain, and from the spathes of the date-palm clusters of dates hanging low. And gardens of grapes, olives and pomegranates, similar yet varied. Look at their fruit when they bear fruit and ripen. Indeed, in these there are signs for a people who believe.﴾ (6:99)

Such glimpses are very abundant in the Qur'an, and such matters do not occur in human thought or in human styles of speech. These aspects of the Qur'an alone are sufficient proof that this Qur'an is from Allah. Even if one sets aside the other proofs, both those within this Book and those in the circumstances in which it was revealed, there are within this Book matters to which the human mind would never turn. Therefore, the doubts of these people were superficial, and they voiced them at a time when only some surahs of the Qur'an had been revealed; the whole Qur'an was not yet complete. Even at that time this distinctive quality was present in the Qur'an. Within it were clear indications that its source is not on earth, but in heaven.

The chiefs of Quraysh felt this in their hearts, and at times they even acknowledged it among themselves. But self-interest blinds a person, and one whose sights are set on worldly gain cannot decide to walk the path of guidance. The Qur'an had foretold regarding such circumstances that they would now level accusations of this kind, saying that it is an ancient falsehood.

Many events have been transmitted in the books of Seerah (the biography of the Prophet ﷺ) that when the leaders of Quraysh spoke among themselves about this matter, they themselves admitted that their statement was wrong.

Ibn Ishaq has transmitted this narration concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, and Utbah ibn Rabi'ah. Of these, he has transmitted the following about the first person:

"Then it happened that some people of Quraysh gathered at the house of al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah. He was an elderly man, and the season of Hajj was approaching, during which delegations from all over the Arab world would come to you, and all the Arabs have heard reports about this man of yours. So gather your opinions and speak with one voice, and do not say contradictory things about him, lest your statements refute one another and you contradict yourselves." They said, "O Abu Abd al-Shams, you speak first and settle a matter for us, and we will act accordingly." He said, "First you tell me what your opinions are." Some said, "We will say that he is a soothsayer." He said, "No, by God, he is not a soothsayer. We have seen soothsayers. His speech is not like the mumbling of soothsayers, nor is there in it the rhymed prose of soothsayers." Then they said, "We will say that he is possessed (majnun)." He said, "He is not possessed either. We have seen the possessed, and we know them. He does not have their fits, nor does he suffer their whisperings, nor is he afflicted by delusions." Some said, "Then let us call him a poet." He said, "He is not a poet. We all know poets, and the forms of poetry: rajaz, hazaj, qarid, maqbud, mabsut. So the Qur'an is not of these." Then they said, "Then let us call him a magician and a sorcerer." He said, "He is not a sorcerer either. We have seen sorcerers; he does not blow as they blow, nor does he tie knots as they do." After that they said, "Abu Abd al-Shams, you tell us what we should call him." He said, "By God, his words are extremely sweet, its roots are deep and its branches spread wide, and there is fruit upon its branches. Whatever you say of it, people will know that it is false. The nearest thing that can be said is that he is a sorcerer who has brought a magic that separates a son from his father, a brother from his brother, a husband from his wife, and a man from his family." So they went away and sat along the roads of Makkah. When the people came for Hajj, whoever came they would speak to him about Muhammad ﷺ and frighten people away from him.

And it is related about Nadr ibn al-Harith that he said: "O people of Quraysh! By God, a calamity has befallen you for which you have no remedy. Muhammad was a small young boy among you, the most beloved of you, the most truthful of you, the most trustworthy of you. When you saw gray hair on his temples and he brought to you what he brought, you said, 'He is a sorcerer.' No, by God, he is not a sorcerer. We have seen sorcerers, and their blowing and their knots we have seen. You said, 'He is a soothsayer.' No, by God, he is not a soothsayer. We have seen soothsayers, and their trances we have seen, and we have heard their rhymed speech. You say, 'He is a poet.' No, by God, he is not; he is not a poet. We have seen poets, and we are acquainted with the forms of poetry: rajaz, hazaj, and so on. You say, 'He is possessed.' We have seen the possessed; he has no fits, nor is he a victim of whisperings, nor are his words confused. O company of Quraysh! Reflect on this matter of yours. By God, I think a great calamity has come upon you..."

The statements of Nadr and Utbah are in complete agreement. It is also possible that this was one single event, which was sometimes attributed to Utbah and sometimes to Nadr. But it is not unlikely that both said something similar, since both were among the notables of Quraysh, and their impressions of the Qur'an were alike.

The position that Utbah took was narrated earlier by us in the introduction to Surah al-Qalam. His stance regarding the Prophet ﷺ and the Qur'an was very close to that of al-Walid and al-Nadr.

In short, when these people made the accusation that you are a sorcerer or a soothsayer, sometimes they said this out of cunning and deceit, and sometimes they did it merely to create confusion. And they never succeeded in this, because the Qur'an itself was so clear that people understood it as soon as they heard it. Therefore it had no need for an oath, that Allah should swear by things that are known and things that are not known. (According to Sayyid Qutb, the meaning of the verses would be: "I do not swear." But the translation of the Indian scholars is correct: "Nay, I swear.")

Indeed, this is the word of the Messenger of Noble Lineage ﷺ. It is not the speech of a poet, nor the speech of a soothsayer. It is sent down from the Lord of the worlds.

The statement here that this is the word of the Noble Messenger ﷺ does not mean that the Noble Messenger ﷺ composed this speech. The meaning is that this is a different kind of speech. Poets and soothsayers cannot produce such speech; only a Messenger can produce such speech. Allah sent him and revealed this to him, and therefore it was immediately said afterward:

﴿It is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ (96:34)

And these following remarks:

﴿Little is it that you believe﴾ (96:24) ﴿Little is it that you take heed﴾ (96:24). Their purpose is that you do not believe at all, and you do not take heed at all. This manner of expression was common in the Arabic language for complete negation, where complete negation was expressed by the word "little." It is related in a hadith that the Prophet ﷺ was "little in idle talk," meaning that he did not engage in idle talk at all. Here the intention is complete negation. Otherwise, if someone had even a little faith, and took even a little admonition from the Qur'an, he could not call the Messenger of Allah a poet or a soothsayer. Only an unbeliever and a heedless person could say such a thing about the Prophet ﷺ.

Finally, there comes this terrifying warning: whoever fabricates a falsehood against Allah regarding the faith will be seized by Allah. This threat also negates the one possibility that remains, namely that the Prophet ﷺ might have made this up himself. So Allah says that you are truthful, and if he had fabricated any falsehood against Us, We would have seized him with severity. Among Islamic beliefs, whoever makes even a slight distortion is seized.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 69, verses 44–47:

ولو تقول ... حجزین

The meaning of these verses is that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is truthful and trustworthy even by your own statements. And if he had fabricated any saying from himself in this Word, We would have seized him in Our grip, and since no punishment of God has come upon him, the necessary conclusion is that he is truthful.

This was a positive argumentative proof. But the manner in which it is stated is the style of a complete and dynamic scene. For instance, it appears as if a mightier person seizes someone with his right hand to call him to account, and then severs his life-vein. This is also an extremely severe and impressive scene. It shows how great the power of Allah is and how helpless man is before Him. All human beings are insignificant before Him.

Furthermore, it shows that the Islamic outlook on life, Islamic beliefs, and all argumentation and discussion about religion are matters of great responsibility, and everyone should speak and act about them with responsibility. When such a threat has been given to Muhammad ﷺ, what will be the condition of those who speak carelessly about Islam? Therefore, this is a place of great fear, dread, caution, humility and reverence, and a discourse calling for vigilance.

Now comes the final concluding passage. In it the decisive point is stated: what is the reality of this religion?

And indeed it is a reminder (tadhkirah) for the God-fearing. And indeed We know that among you there are those who deny it. And indeed it is a regret for the disbelievers. And indeed it is the certain truth (haqq al-yaqin).

"This Qur'an can give admonition only to those hearts in which there is some measure of fear of accountability; that is, the reality which the Qur'an has brought must exist within their hearts. The Qur'an reminds them to remember it too, and it stirs their hearts towards it. As for those who do not fear at all, their hearts are heedless and blind, distorted. They are deprived of the light of recognition (ma'rifah) and of admonition, and the Qur'an is of no benefit to them.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 69, verse 49:

"And [indeed] ..................... among you are deniers" (96 : 94). "And We know that some of you are those who deny." But the rejection of some people does not change the reality. In the same way, your act cannot change the facts.

Surah 69, verse 50:

And indeed it is a cause of regret for the disbelievers (69:50). ﴿وَإِنَّهُ لَحَسْرَةٌ عَلَى الْكَافِرِينَ﴾ (69:50). That is, it is a cause of grief for such disbelievers.

This is because the Qur'an raises the standing of the people of faith, while it lowers the status of those who deny it. In the end, the truth is bound to prevail, and those who deny it are bound to be humiliated. This will happen soon, and then it will become a source of regret for them. On the Day of Resurrection too it will be an argument against them, and it will be a cause of regret, because on account of their denial they will be given a severe punishment. Thus it will be a cause of regret for them both in this world and in the Hereafter.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 69, verse 51:

﴿And indeed it is the certain truth (ḥaqq al-yaqīn)﴾ (69:51). Despite the denial of those who deny, it is the truth. It is certain. Not merely certain, but ḥaqq al-yaqīn. Ḥaqq al-yaqīn is a particular form of emphasis, forceful in its wording and emphatic in its meaning. The sense is that it is profound in truthfulness and profound in certainty, and whatever is stated in it is truth and reality. What has been said in each and every verse has God as its source.

This is the nature and temperament of this religion, and its inevitable outcome. It is neither poetry, nor the saying of any soothsayer. Nor is it a fabrication against God. Rather, it has been sent down by the Lord of the worlds, and it is a reminder and admonition for the God-fearing. And it is ḥaqq al-yaqīn.

Now, at the very end, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is given his final instructions. After the preceding discussion, this kind of exhortation comes at the best and most fitting moment. Therefore this is a most timely guidance.

﴿So glorify with the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾

Such glorification (tasbih) includes both the declaration of Allah's purity and the declaration of His greatness. It includes acknowledgment of the truth and affirmation of the truth. It includes servitude ('ubudiyyah) as well as humility and submissiveness (khushu' wa khud'). After that long discussion, in which the great powers of Allah were described and the greatness of the Generous Lord was made known, a consciousness is awakened in the hearts that their Lord is the Mighty.
